open.text:
Let me start with a patient.

He has pneumonia and is on high-flow oxygen. His saturation is holding. There's no ventilator, so there's no plateau, no driving pressure, no number that worries you. Yet he's breathing at thirty-five, his neck muscles working with every breath. And over the next day his lungs get steadily worse.

Who is injuring his lung? There's no machine to blame. He is.

[[Patient self-inflicted lung injury is lung damage caused by the patient's own vigorous breathing effort.]]

This is the other side of the pressure map. So far, the danger was the chest wall hiding a safe lung behind a high plateau. Here it's the reverse. A strong effort hides a dangerously stretched lung behind a low airway pressure.

What is the professor really checking? First, the mechanism, in pressures. Second, how you would detect high drive and effort at the bedside, with numbers. Third, when you stop non-invasive support and intubate. And fourth, the nuance, because the trap here is to say that spontaneous breathing is harmful. It isn't. Vigorous breathing can be.

So here's the plan. First the mechanism. Then how to measure drive and effort. Then the drive index itself. Then when to intubate. And finally, how far you can take the lung's rest on ECMO.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Patient self-inflicted lung injury is lung damage from the patient's own vigorous effort, on NIV, high flow, or assisted modes.]]

Why does it happen? Strong effort makes the pleural pressure very negative, so the transpulmonary pressure and the lung stretch are high, and fluid is pulled into the lung. Pendelluft over-stretches the dependent lung locally.

How do you detect it? A P zero point one above three and a half to four means high drive. The muscle pressure is about three quarters of the occlusion pressure. Large oesophageal swings mean large effort.

The evidence. On NIV, an expired tidal volume above nine and a half millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight predicted failure, in Carteaux's study in 2016.

[[What do I do? Treat what drives the breathing, adjust support and sedation, intubate early if NIV is failing, and paralyse only in severe cases.]]

And the caution. Gentle spontaneous breathing is not harmful. The aim is to control drive, not to abolish breathing.

That's your answer. What it is, why it happens, how you detect it, the evidence, what you do, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Today we kept the lung from being stretched. What about the opposite idea? Taking the collapsed lung and forcing it open, deliberately, with a burst of high pressure. It sounds logical. And when it was finally tested properly, the result surprised everyone.

That's recruitment manoeuvres. Next.

questions.text: Tell us about recruitment manoeuvres.

steps.bridge: Sustained inflation is the classic method, at a cost of hypotension and barotrauma. Next: what ART showed and what guidelines now say →

lesson.text:
There are two ways to do it.

The classic one is a sustained inflation. CPAP of forty centimetres of water, held for thirty to forty seconds. The other is a stepwise, staircase rise in PEEP, climbing to high pressures and then coming back down to a chosen level.

Now the harms. [[Hypotension, barotrauma, and desaturation.]]

Why hypotension? Picture the pressure map again. The high pressure in the chest squeezes the great veins, so venous return falls. And the over-inflated alveoli squeeze the small vessels in their walls, so the right ventricle must pump against a higher resistance. Cardiac output drops.

Why barotrauma? Because the same pressure reaches every open unit. And here's the core problem.

[[The pressure that opens the collapsed lung also over-stretches the lung that's already open.]]

If the lung is recruitable, the high pressure opens a lot of new units, and it may be worth it. If it isn't recruitable, you get all the over-stretch and all the squeeze on the heart, for nothing.

How would you know? You already have the bedside test, from driving pressure. Raise the PEEP and watch. If the compliance rises and the driving pressure falls, the lung is opening. If the driving pressure rises, you're only over-stretching what was already open.

And the card's last line. The ART trial tested stepwise recruitment plus PEEP titrated to the best compliance, against low PEEP. Recruitment gave higher mortality, and more barotrauma.

[[Routine prolonged recruitment is not recommended.]]

So let's look at that trial more closely.

steps.bridge: ART showed harm, and ESICM and ATS advise against prolonged high-pressure manoeuvres. Next: does recruitment help in the operating room →

lesson.text:
ART was published in 2017. One thousand and ten patients with ARDS. One arm got stepwise recruitment up to very high pressures, then PEEP titrated to the best compliance. The other got low PEEP.

The result. Twenty-eight-day mortality was fifty-five point three percent with recruitment, against forty-nine point three without. More barotrauma, and more hypotension.

[[ART: stepwise recruitment plus PEEP titration raised twenty-eight-day mortality, fifty-five point three against forty-nine point three percent.]]

Why? You already know. The lung that didn't recruit got over-stretched, and the high pressure cut venous return and loaded the right ventricle. And one thing the panel likes you to add. Patients weren't selected for how recruitable their lungs were. Everyone got the manoeuvre.

Then the guidelines followed.

{{**ART 2017** (n = 1,010): 28-day mortality **55.3% vs 49.3%**, more barotrauma
**ESICM 2023:** strongly against prolonged high-pressure RMs (≥ 35 cmH₂O for ≥ 1 min); weakly against routine brief RMs
**ATS 2024:** strongly against prolonged RMs}}

The European society, ESICM, in 2023, recommends strongly against prolonged high-pressure manoeuvres, and weakly against routine brief ones. The American Thoracic Society, in 2024, recommends strongly against prolonged manoeuvres.

So is there any role left? Only as expert practice, not a guideline endorsement. A brief, moderate-pressure manoeuvre may be considered in a patient shown to be recruitable, or after an accidental disconnection, when you know the lung has just collapsed.

[[Recruitment is a rescue for selected patients, not a routine.]]

Now, you might think this is only an ICU story. But you've been doing recruitment in the theatre for years.

steps.bridge: With PEEP, recruitment in PROVHILO added hypotension but no benefit. Next: the sepsis targets, read with the newer guidance →

lesson.text:
Two trials in the operating theatre, and they're best understood side by side, because they changed different things.

IMPROVE, by Futier's group. Four hundred patients. One arm got a whole protective bundle: a tidal volume of six to eight, PEEP of six to eight, and recruitment. The other got the old practice: ten to twelve millilitres per kilo, no PEEP, no recruitment. Complications fell from twenty-seven and a half percent to ten and a half. Less atelectasis, less pneumonia, and a hospital stay two days shorter.

PROVHILO kept the low tidal volume in both arms. It changed only one thing. PEEP of twelve with recruitment, against PEEP of two or less without. And there was no difference in lung complications. Just more hypotension, and more vasoactive drugs, with the high PEEP.

{{ | IMPROVE (Futier) | PROVHILO
Compared | VT 6–8 + PEEP 6–8 + RM vs VT 10–12, no PEEP, no RM (n = 400) | PEEP 12 + RM vs PEEP ≤ 2, same low VT
Result | complications **10.5% vs 27.5%** | **no difference**; more hypotension}}

Now read them together. IMPROVE's control arm had two harms at once, big breaths and no PEEP. So it shows the bundle beats old practice, but it can't tell you which part of the bundle mattered. PROVHILO answers that. Once the breaths are small, high PEEP and recruitment add nothing, and they cost blood pressure.

[[Low tidal volume protects. Routinely high PEEP with recruitment in the theatre does not.]]

So the gain in IMPROVE most likely came from the smaller breaths. It's the same story as ART, told in healthier lungs. The high pressure squeezed the heart, and brought no benefit to show for it.

Now the last card, and it's one where you must be careful which guideline you quote.

Sepsis-induced ARDS is ventilated like any ARDS. Each target limits the stretch on the small open lung.

A tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight. A plateau below thirty. Prone ventilation as needed. Intermittent boluses of neuromuscular blocker rather than a routine infusion, because the ROSE trial showed no benefit from routine continuous cisatracurium. And VV ECMO in refractory cases.

Now the recruitment line, and this is where the trap is.

The Surviving Sepsis guideline of 2021 still weakly suggests the traditional, sustained-inflation manoeuvre. And it strongly advises against the incremental PEEP kind, the staircase kind that ART tested.

But the newer ARDS guidelines are stricter. ESICM in 2023 is strongly against prolonged and weakly against brief high-pressure manoeuvres. ATS in 2024 is strongly against prolonged ones.

[[Where the sepsis advice and the newer ARDS guidelines differ, quote the newer ARDS guidelines.]]

{{**SSC 2021:** weakly for traditional RMs; strongly against incremental-PEEP RMs
**ESICM 2023:** strongly against prolonged, weakly against brief high-pressure RMs
**ATS 2024:** strongly against prolonged RMs}}

And the card's last idea is worth a sentence to the panel, because it shows you see the whole patient. Organ cross-talk. Shock leads to fluids. Fluids lead to overload and kidney injury. That worsens the lung. The lung needs ventilation, ventilation brings injury, the injury releases mediators, and the circle closes in multi-organ failure. That's biotrauma again, with the rest of the body joined in.

spine: What it is: a brief high pressure to open collapsed alveoli, then PEEP to hold them open. Sustained inflation (for example **40 cmH2O for 40 s**) or a stepwise rise in PEEP.
Why it can harm: the lung that does not recruit gets over-stretched, and high pressure cuts venous return and loads the right ventricle. Hypotension, barotrauma and desaturation follow.
Evidence: **ART (2017, n = 1,010)**: stepwise recruitment plus PEEP titration raised 28-day mortality, **55.3% vs 49.3%**, with more barotrauma.
Guidelines: **ESICM 2023** strongly against prolonged high-pressure manoeuvres and weakly against routine brief ones. **ATS 2024** strongly against prolonged manoeuvres.
In surgery: PROVHILO (PEEP 12 plus recruitment) showed no fewer complications, only more hypotension.
Caution: the older sepsis advice that allows sustained inflation is outdated. I use recruitment only as a rescue in selected patients, not routinely.

open.text:
Here's an idea that sounds too logical to fail.

The ARDS lung is mostly collapsed. The baby lung is small. So why not open the rest? Give a brief burst of high pressure, pop the collapsed units open, then hold them open with PEEP. A bigger lung, a gentler stretch on every breath. For years, many of us did exactly that.

Then it was tested in a large trial. And the patients who got the aggressive recruitment did worse.

[[A recruitment manoeuvre is a brief high pressure to open collapsed alveoli, followed by PEEP to keep them open. Routine use caused harm.]]

This is a trial question, so the professor wants numbers. But what he's really checking is whether you understand why something so logical went wrong. If you can explain the harm on the pressure map, the trial result stops being a fact to memorise. It becomes what you'd expect.

And there's a second test hidden here. The older sepsis guidance still allows the classic manoeuvre, while the newer ARDS guidance turns against it. Do you know which is current?

So here's the plan. First the methods and their harms. Then the ART trial and the guidelines. Then the operating theatre. And last, how to read the sepsis targets.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[A recruitment manoeuvre is a brief high pressure to open collapsed alveoli, then PEEP to hold them open. Either a sustained inflation, such as forty for forty seconds, or a stepwise rise in PEEP.]]

Why can it harm? The lung that doesn't recruit gets over-stretched, and the high pressure cuts venous return and loads the right ventricle. Hypotension, barotrauma and desaturation follow.

The evidence. ART, in 2017, one thousand and ten patients. Stepwise recruitment plus PEEP titration raised twenty-eight-day mortality, fifty-five point three against forty-nine point three percent, with more barotrauma.

The guidelines. ESICM in 2023, strongly against prolonged high-pressure manoeuvres, and weakly against routine brief ones. ATS in 2024, strongly against prolonged ones.

In surgery, PROVHILO, PEEP of twelve plus recruitment, showed no fewer complications. Only more hypotension.

[[The sepsis advice that allows sustained inflation predates the newer ARDS guidelines. I use recruitment only as a rescue in selected patients, not routinely.]]

That's your answer. What it is, why it harms, the trial, the guidelines, the theatre, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Every patient today had ARDS, or was having surgery. Yet most of the patients you ventilate in the ICU don't have ARDS at all. Do they need protective ventilation too? Or is six millilitres per kilo only for the injured lung?

That's the next question.

questions.text: Lung protective ventilation in patients without ARDS - is it beneficial?

steps.bridge: The rule is 6–8 mL/kg PBW and never above 10. Next: what PReVENT tested in ICU patients without ARDS →

lesson.text:
The rule first. Six to eight millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight. Avoid more than ten. Keep the driving pressure low.

Why would a lung without ARDS need protecting? Because the lung of a ventilated patient is often smaller than it looks. He's lying flat, sedated, often with some lung already collapsed at the bases. Some patients have injured or at-risk lungs from sepsis, aspiration, or a big transfusion. So a large breath goes into less lung than you think, and it can tip a vulnerable lung into injury.

[[Ventilated patients without ARDS often have collapsed or at-risk lung, so large breaths can push them into injury.]]

The first evidence came from a meta-analysis by Serpa Neto in 2012. Twenty studies, about two thousand eight hundred patients, mostly small randomised trials, many of them in surgical patients. Lower tidal volumes were linked with less lung injury, about a third of the risk, and lower mortality, about two thirds of the risk.

{{**Serpa Neto 2012** (20 studies, n = 2,822, mostly small RCTs): lower Vt → lung injury RR 0.33, mortality RR 0.64
**Rule:** 6–8 mL/kg PBW · avoid > 10 · keep ΔP low}}

That's a strong signal. But a meta-analysis of small trials is not a large trial. And the comparison was often against very big breaths, the kind few of us use now.

So someone ran the large trial.

steps.bridge: PReVENT found no difference in ventilator-free days. Next: what the operative trials show →

lesson.text:
That trial was PReVENT, published in 2018. Nine hundred and sixty-one ventilated ICU patients without ARDS.

It compared a low tidal volume, four to six millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight, with an intermediate one, eight to ten. In practice, the low arm started at six and stepped down towards four, and the other started at ten. That's why you'll hear it quoted as six against ten. And the result: no difference in ventilator-free days. Twenty-one days in both arms at day twenty-eight.

[[PReVENT: in patients without ARDS, a low tidal volume gave the same ventilator-free days as an intermediate one. No harm, and no benefit.]]

Now, why might that be? Look at what was actually achieved. About six to seven in the low arm, against about nine in the other. So the trial compared a small breath with a moderate one. Not with the big breaths of ten to twelve that old control arms used, as in IMPROVE.

{{**PReVENT 2018** (n = 961, no ARDS): low 4–6 vs intermediate 8–10 mL/kg PBW
Achieved ≈ 6–7 vs ≈ 9 · ventilator-free days at day 28: **21 vs 21**}}

So the honest reading is this. [[Low tidal volume is proven in ARDS, by ARMA. In lungs without ARDS, it isn't proven to help.]]

What does that mean for you at the bedside? You don't need to force six millilitres per kilo if it causes distress, or needs heavy sedation. But you still avoid large breaths. Above ten is where the old harm lived.

steps.bridge: IMPROVE cut complications with low volume plus PEEP; PROVHILO found high PEEP added nothing. Next: what links them all →

lesson.text: You met these two trials with recruitment. IMPROVE compared a whole protective bundle, low volume, PEEP and recruitment, against big breaths with no PEEP, and cut complications from twenty-seven and a half to ten and a half percent. PROVHILO kept the low volume in both arms and added only high PEEP with recruitment: no benefit, just more hypotension. For this question, read them as one sentence. In the theatre, the small breath protects. Routinely high PEEP adds nothing.

And this card ties them together. You met it with driving pressure. Across seventeen operative trials, about two thousand two hundred patients, a higher driving pressure was linked to more lung complications, about sixteen percent higher odds for each centimetre of water. And PEEP helped only when it lowered the driving pressure. That explains IMPROVE and PROVHILO at once. What protects the lung is a low stretch, not any particular PEEP.

The card's last line, as a fast fact. A high oxygen fraction during surgery made no difference to short-term mortality, and it may increase atelectasis.

spine: What I do: **6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight**, avoid more than **10**, and keep driving pressure low.
Why: ventilated patients without ARDS often have collapsed or at-risk lung, so large breaths can tip them into injury.
Evidence: a **Serpa Neto 2012** meta-analysis linked lower tidal volume with less lung injury. **PReVENT (2018, n = 961)**, 4–6 vs 8–10 mL/kg: ventilator-free days the same.
In surgery: **IMPROVE** (low volume, PEEP and recruitment) cut complications, **10.5% vs 27.5%**. PROVHILO found high PEEP added no benefit, only hypotension.
Driving pressure: a meta-analysis of **17 trials** found it the variable linked to complications. PEEP helps only if it lowers driving pressure.
Caution: no need to force 6 mL/kg if it causes distress or heavy sedation needs. Just avoid large breaths.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient you'll see this week.

A man ventilated after a cardiac arrest, or for a head injury, or for an overdose. His chest X-ray is clear. His oxygenation is fine. He doesn't have ARDS. So does he need six millilitres per kilo? Or can you give him a comfortable, bigger breath?

This is a trial question, and it's a lovely one, because the evidence is genuinely mixed. The professor isn't asking you to recite a rule. He's asking whether you can hold two kinds of evidence together. Older data that say small breaths help. A large trial that found no difference. And operative trials that point at one number.

[[The answer is six to eight millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight, avoiding more than ten, with a low driving pressure.]]

And what the professor is really checking is whether you can say that without overselling it. A resident who says six millilitres per kilo for everyone, always, will be asked about PReVENT. A resident who says it doesn't matter will be asked about IMPROVE.

So here's the plan. First the rule and why it exists. Then the ICU trial. Then the operating theatre. And finally, the number that ties it all together.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[What I do: six to eight millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight, avoiding more than ten, and a low driving pressure.]]

The evidence. A meta-analysis by Serpa Neto in 2012 linked lower tidal volumes with less lung injury and lower mortality. Then PReVENT, in 2018, nine hundred and sixty-one patients, a low against an intermediate tidal volume, found the same ventilator-free days.

In surgery, IMPROVE, with low volume, PEEP and recruitment, cut complications from twenty-seven and a half to ten and a half percent. PROVHILO found that high PEEP added no benefit, only hypotension.

And the number that joins them. A meta-analysis of seventeen operative trials found driving pressure was the variable linked to complications. PEEP helps only if it lowers the driving pressure.

[[The caution: there's no need to force six millilitres per kilo if it causes distress or heavy sedation. Just avoid large breaths.]]

That's your answer. What you do, why, the ICU evidence, the theatre, driving pressure, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. In every lung so far, the danger was too much stretch. A breath too big for the lung it went into. Now picture the opposite problem. A lung that's too big already, with airways so narrow that each breath goes in, but doesn't fully come out before the next one arrives. The gas stacks up, breath after breath, and a hidden pressure builds inside the chest.

That's COPD, and auto-PEEP. And that's where we go next.

questions.text: How do you ventilate COPD / acute severe asthma? What is auto-PEEP?

steps.bridge: Before any tube, NIV is first choice in hypercapnic COPD. Next: if he is intubated, what are we aiming for →
Target pH, not PaCO2, and avoid paralysis. Next: the settings that let a slow lung empty →
Low rate, small breaths, fast flow, long expiration. Next: how do I see trapping on the screen →
Flow not returning to zero means gas is trapped. Next: how do I measure how much →
An end-expiratory hold gives total PEEP; minus set PEEP is auto-PEEP. Next: how do I bring it down →
Lengthen expiration, mainly by cutting rate and minute ventilation. Next: can adding external PEEP help →

spine: What it is: high airway resistance makes a long time constant, so the lung cannot empty before the next breath. Trapped gas leaves pressure at end-expiration: auto-PEEP.
First line: NIV in a COPD exacerbation with pH below 7.35. It cuts intubation risk by 65% and mortality by 46%.
What I set: tidal volume under 8 mL/kg, rate 10 to 14, flow 80 to 100 L/min, I:E 1:3 to 1:5, plateau under 30. Target pH, not PaCO2.
How I check: expiratory flow not reaching zero shows trapping. An end-expiratory hold gives total PEEP; total minus set PEEP is auto-PEEP.
Fixes: cut the rate first, then bronchodilators and steroids. In COPD, external PEEP at about 80% of auto-PEEP eases triggering (the waterfall).
Caution: sudden hypotension after intubation means trapping. Disconnect, let the chest empty, then lower the rate. Avoid paralysis with steroids.

questions.text: Explain APRV.

steps.bridge: A long high pressure with brief releases, so the lung never fully empties. Next: what each of the four settings controls →
P high and T high drive oxygenation; P low and T low clear CO2. Next: what it gains and what it costs →
Spontaneous breathing and comfort, but CO2 depends on the patient. Next: the risks and the evidence →

spine: What it is: a bilevel mode. A long high pressure holds the lung open, with very brief releases to a low pressure. Always a severe inverse ratio.
Settings: P high and T high (several seconds) give oxygenation. P low (often 0) and a short T low, about 0.4 to 0.8 s, clear CO2.
Why so short a release: it ends when expiratory flow falls to 50 to 75% of peak, so gas is trapped on purpose and alveoli stay open.
Gains: the patient breathes freely on top, with better V/Q matching, less sedation and less circulatory compromise.
Caution: release volumes are not controlled, CO2 can rise, and strong efforts on high pressure add hidden stress. No large trial shows lower mortality: a rescue mode, not first-line.

questions.text: How do you manage a bronchopleural fistula on the ventilator?

steps.bridge: A persistent air leak, seen as expired volume below inspired. Next: what drives gas through the hole →
Less pressure and less inspiratory time means less leak, and no suction. Next: what if the leak is too big for that →
Isolate the lung or use jet ventilation in selected cases. Next: can the hole itself be closed →

spine: What it is: a communication between a bronchus and the pleura with an air leak beyond 24 hours. On the ventilator: lost tidal volume and PEEP, and bubbling.
Why it leaks: flow follows the transpulmonary pressure gradient and the time spent in inspiration.
What I do: peak pressure under 30, tidal volume 4 to 6 mL/kg, lowest PEEP, short inspiration, low rate, permissive hypercapnia, spontaneous modes if possible.
Drain: water seal only, no negative suction. Check the tube position and patency.
Large leak: lung isolation with a double-lumen tube or blocker, then independent lung ventilation. Bronchoscopy: glue for defects under 5 mm, valves for distal leaks.
Caution: mortality is high, about 27 to 50%. Evidence for jet ventilation is weak.

questions.text: Define ARDS. What did the 2023 global definition change?

steps.bridge: Four criteria: timing, imaging, origin, oxygenation on PEEP. Next: how is severity graded →
Three bands by P/F, with mortality rising from 27% to 45%. Next: a quick check of those bands →
Same bands; CPAP counts for mild only under Berlin, not the 2023 rules. Next: what Berlin changed from AECC →
Berlin dropped wedge pressure and the term ALI, but still needs a gas and PEEP. Next: what 2023 added →
High flow, S/F and ultrasound now count. Next: the full picture of what changed and why →

spine: What it is (Berlin 2012): within 1 week of an insult, bilateral opacities, oedema not fully explained by the heart or fluid, and P/F 300 or less on PEEP or CPAP of 5 or more.
Grades: mild 201 to 300, moderate 101 to 200, severe 100 or less. Mortality 27, 32 and 45%.
Why PEEP 5: PEEP changes P/F, so a floor makes the ratio comparable. Wedge pressure was dropped; echo is used if no risk factor is present.
2023 adds: non-intubated patients on high flow of 30 L/min or more, or NIV/CPAP of 5 or more. These are not graded.
Also: S/F of 315 or less in place of P/F when SpO2 is 97% or less, and lung ultrasound for bilateral changes.
Resource-limited settings: no PEEP or flow minimum. S/F and ultrasound are enough.

questions.text: How do you titrate PEEP in ARDS?

steps.bridge: PEEP above the lower inflection holds alveoli open; beaking means over-stretch. Next: who actually gains from more PEEP →
Moderate to severe ARDS has more lung to recruit; mild does not. Next: the simplest way to set it →
The table pairs each FiO2 with a PEEP, aiming SpO2 88 to 95%. Next: how to set it for the individual lung →
Oesophageal pressure lets us keep end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure positive. Next: when does that matter most →
A stiff abdomen or chest wall needs more PEEP; set it by best compliance. Next: what the trials showed →
Higher PEEP did not change mortality overall, only in P/F 200 or less. Next: methods, guidelines and the bedside check →
Choose a method, then confirm with driving pressure. Next: should I add a recruitment manoeuvre →

spine: What it is: enough PEEP to keep alveoli open at end-expiration without over-stretching the open lung.
Who benefits: moderate to severe ARDS, P/F 200 or less, has more recruitable lung. Mild ARDS gains nothing and may be harmed.
How: the ARDSNet PEEP-FiO2 table (higher table if moderate to severe); best compliance on a decremental trial; oesophageal pressure keeping end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure 0 or above; EIT.
Bedside check: if raising PEEP lowers driving pressure, lung was recruited. If driving pressure rises, it is over-stretching.
Evidence: ALVEOLI, LOVS and EXPRESS showed no mortality difference. Briel 2010 found benefit only when P/F was 200 or less. EPVent-2 (oesophageal guided) was neutral.
Caution: ATS 2024 suggests higher PEEP without prolonged recruitment manoeuvres. The ART trial showed higher mortality with stepwise recruitment.

questions.text: What oxygen target do you use in ventilated patients?

steps.bridge: FiO2 and mean airway pressure set oxygen; usual PaO2 goal 60 to 80. Next: is ARDS different →
ARDSNet accepted lower: PaO2 55 to 80, SpO2 88 to 95%. Next: what target do we use on ECMO →
Even on ECMO we aim for about 92 to 96%, not 100%. Next: what about sepsis →
Sepsis guidance is uncertain, with a possible harm signal from going low. Next: what the big trials show →

spine: What I aim for: enough, not more. Roughly SpO2 92 to 96%, or 88 to 95% (PaO2 55 to 80) in ARDS.
Why: too little injures organs. Too much causes oxygen toxicity, absorption collapse and vasoconstriction, and does not fix shunt.
Evidence: ICU-ROX, HOT-ICU (90-day mortality 42.9 vs 42.4%) and UK-ROX (35.4 vs 34.9%) found no mortality difference between conservative and liberal.
Caution: in ARDS, lower is not safer. LOCO2 stopped early with a harm signal at PaO2 55 to 70. In sepsis, a post hoc signal suggested harm from conservative oxygen.
Exceptions: carbon monoxide (100%), a pneumothorax being absorbed, and after cardiac arrest, where both hypoxia and hyperoxia are avoided.

questions.text: HFNO vs NIV in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

steps.bridge: HFNO did not cut intubation overall but lowered 90-day mortality. Next: what the sepsis guideline prefers →
Surviving Sepsis suggests high flow over NIV. Next: how do I know high flow is working →
ROX 4.88 or more predicts success; low values at 2, 6 or 12 h predict failure. Next: the quick version and when to act →
High effort and a rising rate on support mean intubate. Next: how do I judge failure on NIV →
HACOR above 5 at 1 hour means over 80% will fail. Next: why does waiting hurt →
Strong efforts injure the lung themselves. Next: how HFNO works and what the guideline says →

spine: What HFNO is: heated, humid gas up to 60 L/min, matching his inspiratory flow, so FiO2 is reliable. It washes out dead space and gives a little PEEP.
Evidence: FLORALI (2015, n = 310): intubation 38% with HFNO, 47% with oxygen, 50% with NIV, not significant. 90-day mortality was lower with HFNO.
Guidelines: ESICM 2023 favours HFNO over conventional oxygen (strong), with no recommendation for or against NIV over HFNO. Surviving Sepsis suggests HFNO over NIV.
How I monitor: ROX index, SpO2/FiO2 divided by rate. 4.88 or more at 2, 6 or 12 h predicts success. On NIV, HACOR above 5 at 1 hour predicts failure.
Caution: vigorous effort causes self-inflicted lung injury. Delayed intubation harms, so decide early if he is failing.

questions.text: What is the role of inhaled nitric oxide in ARDS?

steps.bridge: It dilates vessels only next to ventilated alveoli, so oxygenation rises for 24 to 72 h, but not survival. Next: where it sits among failed therapies →
It sits on the list of therapies with no survival benefit. Next: the V/Q fix that does save lives →

spine: What it does: inhaled, it reaches only ventilated alveoli and dilates the vessels beside them. Blood moves away from shunt, so V/Q improves.
Bonus: it lowers pulmonary artery pressure without systemic hypotension.
Evidence: oxygenation improves for 24 to 72 hours, but there is no mortality benefit.
Harms: methaemoglobinaemia, nitrogen dioxide, rebound pulmonary hypertension on withdrawal, and renal dysfunction.
Where I use it: rescue only, as a short bridge in refractory hypoxaemia or acute right-heart failure. Prone positioning improves V/Q and does improve survival.

questions.text: When will you put this patient on ECMO? (VV-ECMO indications)

steps.bridge: Prone first; ECMO only after optimisation by EOLIA criteria. Next: the full list of indications →
Refractory hypoxaemia, refractory hypercapnia, or a severe air leak. Next: how the trials and ELSO select patients →
EOLIA entry: P/F under 50 for 3 h, under 80 for 6 h, or pH under 7.25. Next: who should not go on →
Seven days of high settings, bleeding in the brain or no exit are contraindications. Next: scores to judge the odds →
RESP predicts VV survival; days ventilated before ECMO count. Next: what the trials showed →
CESAR favoured transfer; EOLIA missed significance with crossover. Next: the whole decision in one place →

spine: First: optimise. Tidal volume 6 mL/kg, plateau 30 or less, PEEP, prone, paralysis if needed.
When (EOLIA criteria): P/F under 50 for over 3 h, or under 80 for over 6 h, or pH under 7.25 with PaCO2 60 or more for over 6 h, with rate 35 and plateau 32 or less.
Who: ventilated for under 7 days, with a reversible cause, at an experienced centre.
When not: irreversible disease with no transplant option, unable to anticoagulate, severe immunosuppression, severe brain injury, moribund.
Evidence: EOLIA (2018, n = 249): 60-day mortality 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09. 28% of controls crossed over; Bayesian re-analysis favours benefit. CESAR also favoured referral.
Guidelines: ESICM 2023 strong for VV-ECMO in selected severe ARDS; ATS 2024 conditional.

questions.text: How do you safely intubate a critically ill patient?

steps.bridge: Sit him up, pre-oxygenate with NIV, use a video laryngoscope. Next: the same bundle for every hypoxaemic patient, with the evidence →

spine: Why it is dangerous: little oxygen reserve (shunt, small FRC), and blood pressure falls with induction and positive pressure.
Oxygen: semi-sitting, pre-oxygenate with NIV, plus apnoeic oxygenation. PREOXI (2024): hypoxaemia 9.1% with NIV vs 18.5% with face mask.
Tube: video laryngoscope first, bougie, most experienced operator, failed-airway plan. DEVICE (2023): first-pass success 85.1 vs 70.8%.
Circulation: fluid if responsive, pressor drawn up or running, cautious dose of ketamine or etomidate.
After: confirm with waveform capnography and start lung-protective settings from the first breath.

questions.text: How will you ventilate this ARDS patient?

steps.bridge: Tidal volume follows lung size, which follows height and sex. Next: where to start and how to adjust →
Start 8, reach 6 mL/kg, plateau 30 or less, rate up to 35. Next: the one number that best predicts survival →
Driving pressure under 15 matters most because it scales to the baby lung. Next: how to set PEEP and oxygen →
Aim SpO2 88 to 95% and move along the PEEP-FiO2 table. Next: should PEEP be higher →
Higher PEEP helps only in moderate to severe ARDS. Next: should I recruit the lung →
Stepwise recruitment raised mortality in ART, so avoid it. Next: the next step if P/F stays low →
Prone early when P/F is under 150, for 16 hours or more. Next: the full starting plan in one place →

spine: Start: work out predicted body weight from height and sex. Tidal volume 6 mL/kg PBW (range 4 to 8), plateau 30 or less, driving pressure 15 or less.
Why: the ARDS lung is small, not stiff. Driving pressure scales the breath to the open lung and was most linked to survival (Amato 2015).
PEEP and oxygen: ARDSNet PEEP-FiO2 table, higher table if moderate to severe. SpO2 88 to 95%. No prolonged recruitment manoeuvres.
CO2: rate up to 35, then accept a high CO2 while pH stays 7.20 or more. If plateau is still over 30, step tidal volume down to 4 mL/kg.
Next steps: prone if P/F stays under 150. PROSEVA: 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%. Then ECMO by criteria.
Evidence: ARMA (2000): 6 vs 12 mL/kg cut mortality from 39.8 to 31.0%. Check for a stiff chest wall and auto-PEEP if pressures stay high.

questions.text: Spotter: CT chest in ARDS.

steps.bridge: The ARDS lung is small, not stiff: only a small part stays aerated. Next: what that looks like on CT →
Aerated front, ground glass middle, collapsed back: gravity on a heavy lung. Next: why the small lung sets our pressure limit →
Driving pressure scales each breath to that small open lung. Next: how turning him moves the collapse →
Prone reopens the back where the blood flows, so V/Q improves. Next: who gets proned and for how long →

spine: What I see: a front-to-back gradient. Aerated, near-normal lung at the front; ground glass in the middle; dense consolidation at the back.
What it means: the front aerated part is the baby lung, small, not stiff (Gattinoni). The back collapses under the weight of the oedematous lung above: the sponge lung.
Why it matters: a normal breath over-stretches the baby lung, so keep tidal volume low and driving pressure under 15.
Proning: the back reopens while perfusion stays mostly at the back, so V/Q improves and shunt falls. Prone if P/F is under 150, for 16 hours or more a day.
Also look for: pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum (barotrauma), effusions and the original cause, such as pneumonia.

questions.text: Why does prone positioning work?

steps.bridge: Only a small part of the lung is open, and gravity decides where. Next: what changes when he is turned prone →
The back reopens where the blood is, and stretch evens out. Next: who to prone and for how long →
P/F under 150 on FiO2 0.6 or more, 16 hours a day. Next: the trial that proved it →
PROSEVA halved 28-day mortality with early, long sessions. Next: when to stop and what can go wrong →

spine: Why it works: the dorsal lung reopens while perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so V/Q matches better and shunt falls.
Also: the pleural pressure gradient becomes more uniform, so stretch spreads evenly: less lung injury. The heart and abdomen no longer press on the lung, and the right ventricle is unloaded.
When: P/F under 150 on FiO2 0.6 or more and PEEP 5 or more, early (within 36 h), sessions of 16 hours or more.
Evidence: PROSEVA (2013, n = 466): 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%. ESICM 2023 recommends it strongly.
Stop: when P/F stays 150 or more on PEEP 10 or less and FiO2 0.6 or less, at least 4 hours after turning supine.
Caution: unstable spine, raised ICP, open abdomen. Watch for facial pressure sores, tube displacement and line loss.

questions.text: What is electrical impedance tomography?
spine: What it is: a belt of 16 to 32 electrodes passes small currents round the chest. Air raises impedance, so it builds a live image of where each breath goes.
Why useful: bedside, continuous, radiation-free and regional (front vs back, left vs right).
PEEP titration: on a decremental PEEP trial, collapse rises as PEEP falls and over-distension rises as PEEP rises. Choose the PEEP where the two curves cross.
Also shows: pneumothorax (sudden loss on one side), pendelluft, the effect of proning, and ventilation-perfusion with a saline bolus.
Caution: it images one slice only, it costs, and no outcome benefit is proven. It is a tool, not a treatment.

questions.text: What is the non-ventilatory management of severe ARDS?

steps.bridge: Prone early and long is the one proven lifesaver. Next: how much fluid should he get →
Keeping him dry gave more ventilator-free days, not lower mortality. Next: should I paralyse him →
ACURASYS helped under deep sedation; ROSE found no benefit. Next: do steroids help →
Early dexamethasone helps; starting after day 14 harms. Next: when does he need ECMO →
ECMO if hypoxaemia or acidosis persists after optimal care. Next: what the ECMO trials showed →
CESAR favoured referral; EOLIA missed significance with crossover. Next: what about inhaled nitric oxide →
It buys oxygenation for a day or two, not survival. Next: where the two guidelines agree and differ →

spine: Prone: P/F under 150, within 36 h, 16 hours or more a day. PROSEVA: 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%. Both guidelines strong for.
Fluids: conservative once out of shock. FACTT: ventilator-free days 14.6 vs 12.1, mortality not different.
Paralysis: ROSE found no benefit (42.5 vs 42.8%). ATS 2024 conditional for early use in severe ARDS; ESICM 2023 against routine infusion.
Steroids: DEXA-ARDS (2020, n = 277), dexamethasone 20 mg then 10 mg: 60-day mortality 21 vs 36%. Do not start 14 or more days after onset.
ECMO: by EOLIA criteria (2018: 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09). ESICM strong, ATS conditional.
Caution: inhaled nitric oxide is rescue only, with no survival benefit. ECCO2R is advised against (REST: 41.5 vs 39.5%, stopped for futility).

questions.text: Tell me the major ARDS trials.

steps.bridge: Small breaths saved lives: the founding trial. Next: what position adds on top →
Prone halved 28-day deaths in severe ARDS. Next: does paralysing the patient help too →
ROSE overturned ACURASYS once controls were lightly sedated. Next: what forcing the lung open did →
Recruitment plus titrated PEEP raised mortality in ART. Next: what keeping the lung dry achieves →
Conservative fluid gave ventilator-free days, not survival. Next: where steroids now stand →
Early dexamethasone helped; late steroids harm. Next: the rescue trial for the sickest →
EOLIA missed its primary end-point but leans to benefit. Next: all of them on one page →

spine: Breath size: **ARMA** (2000, 861 patients): 6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted weight cut mortality **31.0 vs 39.8%**. It founded lung-protective ventilation.
Position: **PROSEVA** (2013): prone ≥16 h a day when P/F <150 cut 28-day mortality **16.0 vs 32.8%**.
Paralysis: **ACURASYS** suggested benefit, but **ROSE** (2019), with lightly sedated controls, found none (**42.5 vs 42.8%**). Not routine.
Opening the lung: **ART** (2017): recruitment with titrated PEEP raised 28-day mortality (**55.3 vs 49.3%**). Fluids: **FACTT**: conservative gave more ventilator-free days, same mortality.
Steroids: **DEXA-ARDS** (2020): early dexamethasone cut 60-day mortality **21 vs 36%**. Rescue: **EOLIA** (2018): ECMO 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09; primary end-point missed.
Practice change: small breaths and early proning I always do; the rest I use selectively. EOLIA's Bayesian re-analysis favours ECMO in the sickest.

questions.text: What is POCUS? Describe lung ultrasound.

steps.bridge: Sliding or B-lines mean the pleura touch; the lung point proves pneumothorax. Next: what airless lung looks like →
Consolidated lung looks like liver; a dynamic air bronchogram means pneumonia. Next: how pleural fluid looks and is measured →
Effusion is a black space, and its depth gives the volume. Next: how BLUE turns these signs into a diagnosis →

spine: What it is: POCUS is bedside ultrasound done by the treating doctor to answer a focused question. Lung ultrasound reads the pleura and its artefacts: A-lines and B-lines.
Pleura: lung sliding or B-lines rule out pneumothorax at that spot. The lung point is 100% specific for it. On M-mode, absent sliding gives the barcode sign.
Consolidation: lung looks like liver, with a shred sign. A dynamic air bronchogram means pneumonia; a static one with a lung pulse suggests atelectasis.
Effusion: anechoic, complex non-septated, complex septated or echogenic. Volume (mL) is about 20 × interpleural distance (mm). Septations show better than on CT.
Evidence: BLUE protocol (Lichtenstein, Chest 2008): profile B = pulmonary oedema; A' plus lung point = pneumothorax; A plus venous clot = PE; A plus PLAPS = pneumonia.

questions.text: How do you diagnose pneumothorax on ultrasound?

steps.bridge: Sliding or B-lines exclude it; the lung point confirms it. Next: where pneumothorax sits in the BLUE scan of the breathless patient →

spine: What I look for: lung sliding at the pleural line. Sliding present = no pneumothorax at that spot.
Rule out: B-lines also exclude pneumothorax there (negative predictive value 100%).
Rule in: the lung point, where sliding meets no sliding, is 100% specific. On M-mode, absent sliding gives the barcode (stratosphere) sign, not the seashore sign.
Evidence: in the BLUE protocol (Lichtenstein, Chest 2008), profile A' (no sliding, A-lines) plus a lung point = pneumothorax.
Caution: absent sliding is not always pneumothorax. Think of mainstem intubation of the other side, pleural adhesions, endobronchial obstruction, diaphragm paralysis.

questions.text: Spotter: lung ultrasound score image.

steps.bridge: The score runs 0–36: higher means more water and less air. Next: which cut-offs predict the weaning outcome →

spine: What it is: the lung ultrasound score. 12 regions (anterior, lateral, posterior; upper and lower; each side), each scored 0–3, total 0–36.
Grades: 0 = A-lines (≤2 B-lines); 1 = ≥3 separated B-lines; 2 = coalescent B-lines; 3 = consolidation. Higher score = more water, less air.
Weaning: score <13 predicts extubation success; >17 predicts failure; 13–17 is uncertain. A score of 18 predicts failure.
Other uses: ARDS severity and follow-up, fluid tolerance (rising B-lines), and PEEP: a falling score shows re-aeration.
Caution: ultrasound cannot see over-distension, so check driving pressure too. Evidence: Bouhemad (AJRCCM 2011) for re-aeration; Soummer (Crit Care Med 2012) for weaning.

questions.text: Spotter - lung ultrasound showing pleural effusion with consolidation.

steps.bridge: Flapping lung in fluid is compression; liver-like lung with moving air is pneumonia. Next: how to grade and size the effusion →
Ultrasound sizes it and sees septations better than CT. Next: how much fluid the chest X-ray misses →

spine: What I see: an anechoic space above the diaphragm (quad sign; sinusoid sign on M-mode), with consolidated, tissue-like lung beneath it.
What it means: lung flapping in fluid with no air bronchograms = compressive atelectasis. Dynamic air bronchograms = pneumonia, so a parapneumonic effusion.
Pattern: anechoic, complex non-septated, complex septated or homogeneously echogenic. Septations, debris or swirl suggest an exudate or empyema.
Size: volume (mL) ≈ 20 × interpleural distance (mm) at the base, end-expiration. A chest X-ray can look normal below 300 mL.
What I do: sample a parapneumonic effusion under ultrasound guidance. Evidence: Lichtenstein (Chest 2009) for the dynamic air bronchogram.

questions.text: Pleural effusion / haemothorax in the ICU — when do you drain?

steps.bridge: Fluid mainly expands the chest wall and flattens the diaphragm, so drainage eases breathing. Next: how ultrasound sizes and grades it →
Septations on ultrasound change the plan. Next: which parapneumonic findings mandate a tube →
Pus, pH <7.20 or septations mean drain now. Next: when blood in the pleura needs a tube →
Haematocrit >50% of blood confirms haemothorax; drain with a large tube. Next: how to drain without re-expansion oedema →

spine: Why drain: raised pleural pressure flattens the diaphragm and can cause RV failure or a tamponade-like picture. Dyspnoea improves after drainage even if gas exchange changes little.
Parapneumonic: drain if pus, positive Gram stain, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, LDH >1000 or septations. Small-bore if no septations; large-bore if septated.
Haemothorax: pleural haematocrit >50% of blood; massive if >1.5 L. Use a 28–30 Fr drain in the mid-axillary line. Do not insert one if aortic dissection or transection is suspected.
How fast: no faster than 500 mL/h, maximum 1.5 L, to avoid re-expansion oedema (higher risk if collapsed >3 days). Treat it with CPAP 5–10 cmH2O and oxygen.
Removal: lung expanded and output <100 mL/day; for parapneumonic effusion, sepsis resolved and <200 mL/day.

questions.text: What is diaphragm ultrasound and how does it help weaning?

steps.bridge: Excursion <10 mm or thickening fraction under about 30% means a weak diaphragm. Next: how it ranks beside the other ultrasound predictors →
Diaphragm, lung score and LV function each predict outcome; excursion <10 mm means a weak diaphragm. Next: what to scan at each weaning step →

spine: What it is: bedside ultrasound of the diaphragm. Excursion is how far the dome moves; thickening fraction is how much the muscle thickens as it contracts.
Excursion: curved probe below the right costal margin, liver as the window, M-mode. Excursion <10 mm on quiet breathing = dysfunction and predicts weaning failure.
Thickening: linear probe at the zone of apposition, mid-axillary line. TF = (end-inspiratory − end-expiratory) ÷ end-expiratory × 100. TF ≥30–36% predicts success.
What I do: measure during the breathing trial or on very low support. Scan before the trial for risk, during it to predict, and after a failure to find the cause.
Evidence: Kim (Crit Care Med 2011) set the <10 mm cut-off; DiNino (Thorax 2014) the thickening fraction. Caution: ventilator support moves a diaphragm that is not working.

questions.text: Classify patient–ventilator asynchrony.

steps.bridge: Asynchrony sorts by phase: trigger, flow and cycling; trigger is 80%. Next: how we put a number on it →
An index >10% is significant and affects about a quarter of patients. Next: does it change outcome →

spine: What it is: a mismatch between the patient's effort and the ventilator breath, classified by the phase where it happens.
Trigger: ineffective effort, double trigger, auto-trigger, reverse trigger. This group is 80%; ineffective effort is the commonest single type.
Flow: flow starvation and insufficient pressurisation. Cycling: premature (patient's inspiration longer than the ventilator's) or delayed (ventilator's longer).
Measure: asynchrony index = asynchronous events ÷ (ventilator breaths + wasted efforts) × 100. Above 10% is significant; Thille found it in 24%.
Evidence: Thille 2006: index >10% meant ventilation 25 vs 7 days and tracheostomy 33% vs 4%. Blanch 2015: ICU mortality 67% vs 14%.

questions.text: What is double triggering? How is it different from reverse triggering?

steps.bridge: Double triggering is the patient outlasting the machine's inspiratory time. Next: reverse triggering, where the machine starts the effort →
Reverse triggering is machine-led, in deep sedation, and also stacks breaths. Next: the one fix for each asynchrony →

spine: Double triggering: two inspirations with no expiration between. The ventilator's inspiratory time is shorter than the patient's, so the continuing effort triggers a second breath.
Reverse triggering: the ventilator breath triggers the patient's effort. Seen in deeply sedated patients on controlled modes, often entrained 1:1, 1:2 or 1:3.
The difference: in double triggering the patient starts it; in reverse triggering the machine does. Reverse triggering is confirmed on oesophageal pressure or diaphragm EMG.
Why it matters: both stack breaths, so delivered volume can almost double (350 becomes 650 mL). Reverse triggering also makes plateau pressure unreliable.
What I do: for double triggering, increase inspiratory time or tidal volume, lower the cycle-off %, switch to pressure support, or sedate.

questions.text: What are the newer ventilator modes — NAVA, PAV, closed-loop?

steps.bridge: Closed-loop modes differ in what sets the pressure and whether they wean. Next: PAV, which follows the patient's flow →
PAV gives a fixed share of the work but needs a triggering patient. Next: NAVA, which reads the diaphragm directly →
NAVA runs on diaphragm electrical activity, so leaks and auto-PEEP do not matter. Next: what both gain over pressure support →
Both improve synchrony and prevent over-assistance; NAVA has more double triggers. Next: ASV, which also works in passive patients →
ASV picks rate and volume for minimum work with Otis' formula. Next: how INTELLiVENT closes the whole loop →

spine: What they are: modes where the ventilator adjusts support from a patient signal, instead of fixed settings.
PAV: pressure in proportion to instantaneous flow and volume; set PEEP, FiO2 and % support. Needs a triggering patient; leaks can cause runaway over-assistance.
NAVA: diaphragm electrical activity from a nasogastric electrode triggers, sizes and cycles the breath; pressure = NAVA level × EAdi. Needs intact drive and phrenic nerves.
ASV: set %MinVol, PEEP and FiO2; Otis' formula picks the rate for minimum work, driven by the expiratory time constant. Works in passive patients and weans.
INTELLiVENT-ASV: fully closed loop. End-tidal CO2 sets ventilation, SpO2 sets PEEP and FiO2, and it runs an automatic breathing trial. SmartCare also weans automatically.
Caution: better synchrony, comfort and less sedation, but few outcome data.

questions.text: Sedation and sedation scores — how do you sedate a ventilated patient?

steps.bridge: Pain is everywhere in the ICU and drives delirium; self-report comes first. Next: how to score pain when the patient cannot speak →
BPS >5 or CPOT >2 means pain. Next: how PADIS treats it before any sedative →
Opioids first, spared by paracetamol, ketamine or gabapentinoids. Next: how to score the depth of sedation →
RASS runs from +4 to −5 by eye contact and response. Next: what depth PADIS asks us to aim for →
Aim light, RASS −2 to +1, with propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. Next: which drug has which pitfall →
Midazolam accumulates, propofol risks PRIS, dexmedetomidine slows the heart. Next: how sedation links to weaning →
Pairing awakening with a breathing trial improved 1-year survival. Next: the bundle that ties pain, sedation and delirium together →

spine: Principle: analgesia first, then the least sedation needed. Assess pain by self-report (0–10 scale), or by BPS (pain if >5) or CPOT (pain if >2).
Pain: opioids are the mainstay. Spare them with paracetamol, nefopam, low-dose ketamine or gabapentinoids. Avoid routine NSAIDs and IV lidocaine.
Target: light sedation, RASS −2 to +1 (Riker SAS 3–4), by daily interruption or a nurse-led protocol. Use BIS only when scales cannot be used, as in paralysis.
Drugs: propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. Midazolam accumulates and causes delirium; propofol risks PRIS above 4–5 mg/kg/h; dexmedetomidine causes bradycardia.
Evidence: awakening paired with a breathing trial (ABC trial) improved 1-year survival. Delirium on the day of the first trial means more extubation failure (40% vs 25%).
Bundle: ABCDEF: pain, both awakening and breathing trials, choice of drugs, delirium, early mobility, family. Avoid physical restraints.

questions.text: What is the PADIS guideline approach to sedation?

steps.bridge: PADIS means analgesia first and light sedation without benzodiazepines. Next: the trials behind going light →
Daily interruption and paired awakening and breathing trials shortened ventilation and saved lives. Next: what this means at the first weaning trial →
Delirium at the first trial raises extubation failure; paired trials help. Next: how the ABCDEF bundle puts it into practice →

spine: What it is: PADIS 2018 covers pain, agitation and sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep. The core rule: analgesia first, then light sedation.
Target: RASS −2 to +1, by daily interruption or nurse-protocolised targets. Propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. No physical restraints unless essential.
Evidence: Kress 2000: daily interruption shortened ventilation and ICU stay. ABC trial (Girard 2008): paired awakening and breathing trials lowered 1-year mortality.
SLEAP 2012: nurse-protocolised light sedation works as well as daily interruption; there is no need to add one to the other.
Bundle: ABCDEF, plus non-drug delirium prevention: protect sleep, reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, early mobility, family.
Caution: deep sedation still has a place: severe early ARDS, paralysis, raised ICP, status epilepticus.

questions.text: Dexmedetomidine versus propofol - what is the evidence?

steps.bridge: Propofol is fast on and off but drops pressure; dexmedetomidine spares breathing but slows the heart. Next: what PADIS prefers →
PADIS puts both ahead of benzodiazepines for light sedation. Next: what the head-to-head trials actually show →

spine: Pharmacology: propofol is fast on and off but causes hypotension and PRIS. Dexmedetomidine is an α2 agonist (0.2–1.5 µg/kg/h): no respiratory depression, but bradycardia.
Guideline: PADIS prefers propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines, for light sedation (RASS −2 to +1).
Evidence: SPICE III (2019, about 4,000): early dexmedetomidine, same 90-day mortality (29.1% each), more bradycardia and hypotension. MENDS2 (2021, sepsis): no difference.
More evidence: A2B (JAMA 2025, n = 1,404): dexmedetomidine or clonidine vs propofol: no faster extubation, more agitation and severe bradycardia, same 180-day mortality.
What I do: propofol as the default. Dexmedetomidine for light sedation, agitated delirium blocking extubation, and non-intubated patients. Avoid it with bradycardia or heart block.

questions.text: How do you diagnose and manage delirium in the ICU?

steps.bridge: Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention from brain inflammation and transmitter imbalance. Next: the arousal scale we check first →
RASS sets the arousal level before we test the content of thought. Next: the four CAM-ICU features →
CAM-ICU positive = 1 + 2 + (3 or 4). Next: the shift-long alternative, ICDSC →
ICDSC ≥4 is delirium; 1–3 is subsyndromal. Next: the full approach, from cause to drugs →
Find the cause and treat without drugs; haloperidol does not shorten delirium. Next: the non-drug bundle in detail →
Non-drug measures and ABCDEF are the treatment. Next: which drugs have been tried and failed →
Antipsychotics failed, benzodiazepines worsen it, dexmedetomidine has a niche. Next: the exact PADIS rulings →

spine: What it is: an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness. The commonest acute encephalopathy in the ICU; hypoactive is the commonest and most missed type.
Diagnose: screen every shift. CAM-ICU: acute change or fluctuation + inattention + either altered consciousness or disorganised thinking. Or ICDSC ≥4 of 8.
Find the cause: hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic upset, withdrawal, drugs (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics), urinary retention, pain, sleep loss.
What I do: non-drug first: reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, sleep, early mobility, family, light sedation. Avoid benzodiazepines unless it is withdrawal.
Evidence: AID-ICU (2022, n = 1,000): haloperidol = placebo for days alive out of hospital at 90 days. MIND-USA (2018): haloperidol or ziprasidone = placebo.
Drugs: no routine antipsychotics. Dexmedetomidine for agitated delirium that stops extubation (DahLIA 2016). A short antipsychotic course only for distress or danger.

questions.text: What is the role of inhaled volatile sedation in the ICU?
spine: What it is: isoflurane or sevoflurane given through the ventilator circuit by a reflector such as AnaConDa or MIRUS, fed by a syringe pump, with gas monitoring.
Why: fast on and off, little accumulation, bronchodilation and less opioid use. Isoflurane is licensed for ICU sedation in Europe.
Limits: added dead space raises CO2 with small tidal volumes; scavenging and cost; malignant hyperthermia; prolonged sevoflurane can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Evidence: SESAR (JAMA 2025, n = 687, ARDS): sevoflurane vs propofol gave fewer ventilator-free days and higher 7-day mortality (19.4% vs 13.5%).
What I do: not for routine use in ARDS. Keep it for refractory status asthmaticus, or when IV sedation is failing.

questions.text: Weaning indices and classification of weaning.

steps.bridge: Readiness is a checklist: oxygenation, circulation, mechanics, mentation. Next: the best-known single index, RSBI →
RSBI <105 is sensitive but not specific, so it screens rather than decides. Next: the other indices and their cut-offs →
Drive, strength and load can each be indexed, but none is perfect. Next: how patients are grouped by their weaning course →
This is the ICC 2007 (Boles) system: simple, difficult, prolonged. Next: how WIND fills its gaps →
WIND counts from the first attempt and includes everyone, so it predicts mortality. Next: what helps right around extubation →

spine: Readiness: cause resolved, SaO2 >90% on FiO2 ≤0.4 with PEEP ≤8, stable circulation, awake with a cough. Then screen with an index.
Indices: RSBI = rate ÷ tidal volume (L); <105 predicts success (sensitivity 97%, specificity 64%). Others: P0.1 below 4–5, CROP >13, integrative weaning index ≥25.
Classification: ICC 2007 (Boles): simple = extubated after the first trial; difficult = up to 3 trials or 7 days; prolonged = more than 3 trials or more than 7 days.
WIND (Béduneau 2017): counts from the first separation attempt. Short within 1 day, difficult 1–7 days, prolonged >7 days, group 0 never tried. Mortality rises by group.
Caution: RSBI is falsely low on CPAP or pressure support, so measure it unassisted over 1 minute.

questions.text: How do you do an SBT? Which method is better?

steps.bridge: Screen daily: oxygenation, circulation, mechanics, mentation. Next: the bedside index before the trial →
RSBI <105 says try; the trial itself decides. Next: how to run the trial →
T-piece or PS 5–8 for 30 minutes, 120 in COPD; a large RCT now settles the method. Next: what that trial showed →
PSV 8 for 30 minutes got more patients extubated than a 2-hour T-piece. Next: when to call a trial failed →
Stop for poor gas exchange, fast breathing, unstable circulation or distress. Next: when the harder T-piece test is better →
In obesity, a T-piece mimics post-extubation work; extubate to NIV. Next: the COPD extubation standard →

spine: Who: daily screen. Cause improving, P/F ≥150 on FiO2 ≤0.4 and PEEP ≤8, stable without high-dose pressors, awake, can cough. RSBI <105 supports trying.
How: pressure support 5–8 cmH2O with zero or low PEEP for 30 minutes, or a T-piece for 30–120 minutes. Use 120 minutes in COPD and high-risk patients.
Fail if: RR >35, SpO2 <90%, heart rate >140 or up 20%, systolic BP >180 or <90, agitation, sweating, accessory muscles. Then rest, find the cause, retry in 24 hours.
Evidence: Subirà (JAMA 2019, n = 1,153): PSV 8 with zero PEEP for 30 minutes vs a 2-hour T-piece: successful extubation 82.3% vs 74.0%, same reintubation.
Which is better: PSV for most. The T-piece is the harder test and mimics post-extubation effort: prefer it if cardiac failure on weaning is suspected, and in obesity.
After: extubate COPD to NIV; it lowers reintubation and ICU mortality.

questions.text: Early versus late tracheostomy.

steps.bridge: Tracheostomy is a tool for difficult and prolonged weaning. Next: does doing it early help →

spine: What it is: the timing question for tracheostomy in difficult or prolonged weaning. TracMan defined early as day 1–4 and late as day 10 or later.
Evidence: TracMan (JAMA 2013, n = 909): 30-day mortality 30.8% vs 31.5%, no difference; fewer sedation days with early. Only about half of the late group ever needed one.
More evidence: SETPOINT2 (JAMA 2022, stroke): early (≤5 days) gave no better 6-month function. Meta-analyses: early may cut sedation and ventilator days, not mortality.
What I do: decide when weaning is clearly prolonged, around day 7–10. Go earlier in high cervical cord injury or severe brain injury needing airway protection.
Technique: percutaneous and surgical have similar mortality. Percutaneous is bedside, quicker, fewer wound infections. Surgical for difficult anatomy, coagulopathy, unstable spine.

questions.text: How do you prevent post-extubation failure?

steps.bridge: Prevention starts with a proper breathing trial; high-risk COPD gets NIV afterwards. Next: the airway and NIV checks around extubation →
The cuff leak test flags stridor risk; NIV can be facilitative or prophylactic. Next: who gets high-flow and who gets NIV →
Low risk gets high-flow; high risk gets NIV with high-flow. Next: why COPD goes straight to NIV →
In COPD, extubation to NIV lowers reintubation and ICU mortality. Next: the obese patient, the other NIV group →

spine: What it is: spotting the high-risk patient first: age >65, heart failure, COPD, BMI >30, APACHE II >12, weak cough or many secretions, failed first trial, hypercapnia.
Airway: cuff leak test; a leak <110 mL means stridor risk. Give methylprednisolone 20 mg 4-hourly, starting 12 hours before extubation.
Low risk: high-flow nasal oxygen for 24 hours (Hernández 2016: reintubation 4.9% vs 12.2%).
High risk: NIV alternating with high-flow (HIGH-WEAN 2019: reintubation 11.8% vs 18.2%). COPD, hypercapnic or obese patients: NIV straight after extubation.
Caution: once respiratory failure is established, do not use NIV to delay reintubation (Esteban 2004: higher mortality).

questions.text: What is ICU-acquired weakness?

steps.bridge: ICU-AW is symmetrical weakness, MRC <48/60; nerve studies split CIP from CIM. Next: where it sits among neuromuscular causes →
CIP is a conduction problem; CIM and diaphragm dysfunction are peripheral. Next: what happens to the diaphragm itself →
Diaphragm dysfunction starts by 48 hours and is in 80% of ICU-AW. Next: how it fits among all causes of weaning failure →
Polyneuromyopathy is one of many weaning failure causes. Next: steroids, a risk factor seen in an ARDS trial →
Late steroids in LaSRS brought more neuromyopathy. Next: the prevention that works, early mobilisation →
Mobilisation reduces ICU-AW, and ventilation is no bar to it. Next: what survivors still carry years later →

spine: What it is: diffuse, symmetrical limb weakness arising in the ICU with no other cause; MRC sum score <48/60 in an awake, cooperative patient. It affects 25–50%.
Types: CIP is axonal, with low motor and sensory amplitudes and distal sensory loss. CIM has low motor but normal sensory amplitudes and weak direct muscle stimulation. Often both.
Why: sepsis and multi-organ failure, hyperglycaemia, immobility, long ventilation, steroids, neuromuscular blockers, early parenteral nutrition.
What I do: avoid hyperglycaemia, keep sedation light, mobilise early (ventilation and low-dose pressors are not contraindications), avoid early parenteral nutrition.
Evidence: Herridge: 109 ARDS survivors at 5 years. Lungs near normal, but weakness persisted; 6-minute walk 76% of predicted. LaSRS: late steroids, more neuromyopathy.
Caution: it explains weaning failure on the capacity side. Diaphragm dysfunction starts by 48 hours, is present in 80%, and correlates poorly with limb MRC.

questions.text: What is the approach to a patient who fails weaning?

steps.bridge: Each weaning group has typical delays, from system failures to chronic organ failure. Next: the respiratory load side →
Load is elastic (stiff lung or chest) or resistive (airways, tube). Next: the capacity side, the neuromuscular causes →
Capacity fails at drive, conduction or muscle level. Next: the heart, the cause most often missed →
Removing positive pressure raises LV preload and afterload, so LVEDP rises. Next: how to prove weaning-induced oedema →
Echo, leg raising and rising plasma protein confirm it; diuretics treat it. Next: what ultrasound adds at each step →
Ultrasound flags risk before, predicts during and finds the cause after a failure. Next: how to manage difficult and prolonged weaning →

spine: Approach: weaning failure is a load–capacity imbalance. Work through respiratory load, neuromuscular capacity, the heart, then metabolic and mental factors.
Load: elastic (oedema, pneumonia, auto-PEEP, effusion, obesity) or resistive (bronchospasm, secretions, narrow tube). Capacity: sedatives, metabolic alkalosis, CIP, CIM, low phosphate.
Heart: losing positive pressure raises LV preload and afterload. Suspect it in left heart disease with COPD. Echo E/A >0.95 and E/e' >8.5, or plasma protein rise >6%, support it.
What I do: ultrasound after a failed trial for high filling pressure or derecruitment. Treat the cause: diuretics resolved 60% of difficult weaning; BNP-guided fluids shorten it.
Then: optimal assistance with pressure support, early mobilisation, consider tracheostomy. If prolonged: rehabilitation, cuff-down trials, speaking valve, home ventilation.

questions.text: What is the role of steroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia?
spine: What I do: give hydrocortisone to adults in the ICU with severe bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, but not in influenza.
Evidence: CAPE COD (NEJM 2023, n = 800): hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 4 or 8 days, then tapered: 28-day mortality 6.2% vs 11.9%, fewer intubations and vasopressor starts.
Other trial: ESCAPe (2022, methylprednisolone) showed no significant mortality difference.
Guideline: SCCM 2024 recommends corticosteroids for adults in hospital with severe bacterial CAP (strong, moderate certainty); no recommendation for less severe CAP.
Caution: CAPE COD excluded influenza and septic shock already on vasopressors. Avoid steroids in influenza; take care with aspergillosis risk; watch glucose and secondary infection.

MV01|VENT-10.intro:
The ventilator can only push. In a passive patient the lung ties pressure, volume and flow together: pressure = flow × resistance + volume ÷ compliance + PEEP. Fix the pressure, and the lung decides volume and flow. Fix the volume (and with it the flow), and the lung decides the pressure. That is why only one can be the control.
See it: squeezing a balloon through a straw. Fix how hard you squeeze, and the straw and the balloon decide how much goes in.
why: b
Pressure fixed: a stiffer lung or a narrower tube now lets less volume in, so volume and flow vary.
c
Volume fixed: the machine pushes whatever pressure it takes, so a stiffer lung shows as a higher pressure.
MV01|VENT-10.cap: Airway pressure is three layers stacked: pushing through the tubes, stretching the lung, and PEEP.

MV02|MODE-07.intro:
Every breath answers two questions: what is held at a ceiling during the breath (the limit) and what ends it (the cycle). The limit is flow in volume control and pressure in the other two. Volume control ends when the set volume is in; pressure control when the set time is up. Pressure support has neither, so it ends when the patient's own inspiratory flow falls, usually to 25% of its peak.
See it: a tap that shuts at a full glass, a kitchen timer, and a straw that stops when the drinker stops sucking.
why: Because pressure support ends on flow, it follows the patient. In COPD, where flow falls slowly, the cycle is often set higher (40–50% of peak) so the breath ends sooner and leaves time to breathe out.

MV02|MODE-03.intro:
In volume control the machine drives a constant flow, so pressure keeps climbing as the lung fills and peaks at the end. In pressure control the machine holds one pressure. Flow is fastest at the start, when the gap between machine and alveoli is biggest, and falls as the alveoli fill. Holding the pressure for the whole breath raises the average pressure, even with a lower peak.
See it: volume control is a ramp; pressure control is a box.
why: b
Decelerating flow: flow = pressure gap ÷ resistance, and the gap shrinks as the alveoli fill.
d

Mean airway pressure is the area under the pressure curve. For the same breath, the pressure-control box peaks lower but stays high for the whole breath, so it holds more area than the volume-control ramp. Mean airway pressure, with FiO₂, is a main driver of oxygenation.

MV02|MODE-09.intro:
In assist-control every trigger gets a full set breath, not a small one. A breathless or anxious patient who triggers fast gets a full breath each time, so minute ventilation climbs and CO₂ falls. If the next breath arrives before the last one is out, breaths stack on top of each other.
See it: every knock on the door lets in a whole crowd.
why: d
Hyperventilation: ventilation = the patient's rate × the machine's full tidal volume, so a fast rate overshoots.
d

Stacking: a strong effort outlasts the set breath and triggers a second one before the first is out, so the lung gets nearly double the volume (barotrauma risk). A fast rate also shortens expiration and leaves gas behind (auto-PEEP).

MV01|VENT-03.intro:
During the breath the ventilator's pressure does two jobs: pushing gas through the tubes, which needs flow, and holding the lung stretched, which needs volume. An inspiratory hold stops the flow, so the pushing part vanishes and only the stretch is left: that is the plateau. Peak to plateau is the airway part; plateau to PEEP is the lung-and-chest part.
See it: peak = push + stretch; plateau = stretch alone.
why: c
Resistance = pressure ÷ flow, so divide the pushing part (peak − plateau) by the set flow in L/s.
d
Compliance = volume ÷ pressure, so divide the tidal volume by the stretch part (plateau − PEEP). If auto-PEEP is present, use total PEEP.
MV01|VENT-03.cap: Peak = resistive + elastic + PEEP. The hold removes the resistive layer and leaves the plateau.

MV01|VENT-04.intro:
Compliance is how much volume each cmH₂O of pressure buys. In early ARDS the lung that is still open behaves roughly normally; there is just far less of it. The same pressure fills a smaller space, so compliance falls. So in early ARDS a low compliance mostly means a small lung, not a stiff one; in fibrosis the lung really is stiff.
See it: the same push into one balloon instead of three.
why: c
On a ventilator the patient is supine and sedated, with some lung collapsed, so the measured value is lower than in an upright person breathing on his own.
d
Lung and chest wall are stretched together, so the total is lower than either alone. A stiff chest wall (obesity, a tense abdomen) lowers total compliance even when the lung is fine.

MV01|VENT-05.intro:
Resistance depends mostly on the airway's radius. In smooth flow it rises with the fourth power of narrowing: halve the radius and you need about sixteen times the pressure for the same flow. That is why an endotracheal tube, narrower than the trachea, raises resistance, and why secretions or bronchospasm show quickly as a higher peak pressure.
See it: the same flow forced through a thinner straw.
why: a
Resistance = pressure ÷ flow, so the same peak-to-plateau gap at a different flow means a different resistance. Always state the flow.

MV01|VENT-08.intro:
Peak contains both push and stretch; plateau contains only stretch. So if only the peak rises, the problem is in the pushing path: the tube or the airways. If both rise together, the stretch has risen: the lung or chest has become stiffer or smaller. If both fall, gas is escaping.
See it: the gap is the airway; the plateau is the lung.
why: b
Pneumothorax and mainstem intubation belong here: they shrink the lung available to the same breath, so its stretch rises.

MV02|MODE-04.intro:
Breathing out is passive: gas leaves as the stretched lung recoils, and narrowed airways slow it down. So the expiratory curve is low (a capped peak) and long (slow emptying). If the next breath starts before expiratory flow reaches zero, some gas is still in the lung. That trapped gas keeps pressure in the alveoli at the end of expiration: auto-PEEP.
See it: a bath still draining when the tap is turned on again.
why: The fix is more time to breathe out and less gas to empty: lower the rate first, then shorten inspiration or reduce the tidal volume.

MV03|ASYN-04.intro:
To trigger a breath, the patient must pull the airway pressure or flow past the set threshold. With auto-PEEP the alveoli already sit above the set PEEP, so his effort must first cancel the trapped pressure before the ventilator notices anything. Weak efforts never get there, and the breath is missed.
See it: knocking on a door with a crowd leaning against it.
why: c
Too much support causes it too: big breaths lower the drive and leave less time to empty, so the next efforts are weaker and start against trapped gas.
d
COPD: floppy lungs and narrow airways empty slowly, so trapping is commonest.

MV03|ASYN-09.intro:
In volume control the flow is fixed. If the patient wants more flow than the machine gives, his own pull lowers the airway pressure during the breath, so the pressure curve sags (scoops) instead of rising smoothly. He is working hard against a machine that will not speed up.
See it: a waiter pouring slowly while you gulp.
why: b
In pressure control flow follows the pressure gap, and the patient's pull widens that gap, so flow rises to meet his demand.
d

Rise time sets how fast the valve opens at the start. Too fast for a weak demand overshoots (a spike); too slow for a strong demand under-fills early (a scoop). In COPD a fast rise puts the volume in early and leaves more time to breathe out.

RESP01B|ARDS-25.intro:
The ventilator sees only airway pressure. Part of it stretches the lung; the rest moves the chest wall. Only the lung's share injures the lung: alveolar minus pleural pressure, the transpulmonary pressure. A stiff or heavy chest wall takes a bigger share, so the same plateau can mean much less stress on the lung.
See it: blowing up a balloon inside a tight jar.
why: c
Pleural pressure cannot be measured at the bedside, so oesophageal pressure stands in for it.
RESP01B|ARDS-25.cap: The ventilator shows airway pressure; the lung feels airway minus pleural. A stiff chest wall takes part of it (A); a strong breath makes pleural pressure negative and adds to it (B).

RESP01B|ARDS-26.intro:
In ARDS much of the lung is shut, so the breath goes into the small part that is open. Compliance tells you how big that open part is. Dividing the breath by compliance shows how hard you are stretching what is actually open. Two patients on the same mL/kg can have very different stretch.
See it: the same breath, into a small lung or a big one.
why: c

In Amato's re-analysis of trials, changes in tidal volume or PEEP were linked to survival only when they lowered driving pressure. The likely reason: driving pressure tracks the stretch of the open lung better than mL/kg does. It includes the chest wall too, so it is not pure lung stress.

RESP01B|ARDS-27.intro:
Each breath delivers energy to the lung. Mechanical power is that energy per breath multiplied by the breaths per minute. Doubling the rate doubles the power; a bigger breath raises it even faster, because it adds both volume and pressure.
See it: a hammer blow struck more often, or swung harder; swinging harder costs more.
why: b

Energy = volume × average pressure during inflation. PEEP and the resistive part are there the whole time; the elastic part climbs from 0 to ΔP, so it averages ½ΔP. Peak − ½ΔP is that average; × tidal volume × rate gives power; 0.098 converts to joules.

RESP01B|ARDS-18.intro:
The lung is injured by being stretched too far, by snapping open and shut each breath, and by the inflammation that follows. Strain is the stretch relative to resting size: tidal volume divided by the volume already in the lung at end-expiration. In ARDS that resting volume is small, so a normal breath is a large strain.
See it: 500 mL into a 1-litre lung is twice the stretch of 500 mL into a 2-litre lung.
why: b
Barotrauma: high transpulmonary pressure ruptures alveoli at their base; air tracks along the vessels into the mediastinum or pleura.
c
Atelectrauma: unstable units snap open and shut with each breath, and the shear at their edges injures them. PEEP keeps them open.
d
Biotrauma: injured lung releases mediators into the blood, which is why ventilator injury can cause failure of distant organs.
e
Ergotrauma: injury tracks the total energy delivered per minute (mechanical power), not any single pressure.

MV01|VENT-01.intro:
The lung always wants to recoil inwards and the chest wall wants to spring outwards. Pulling in opposite directions, they create a slight suction in the pleural space, about −5 at rest. Breathing in, the diaphragm pulls the chest wall out further and the lung is stretched more, so the suction deepens to about −10. Air moves only down a gradient, so alveolar pressure must dip just below atmosphere to draw air in and rise just above it to push air out.
See it: two springs hooked together, one pulling in and one pulling out; the gap between them is under suction.
why: a
More negative at end-inspiration because the stretched lung recoils harder, and the muscles must out-pull that recoil to hold the bigger volume.
b
Only a small gap (about 1 cmH₂O) is needed because the airways of a healthy lung offer little resistance. At the end of each phase flow stops and alveolar pressure returns to zero.
c
